question.prompt:
Each square in a \(5 \times 5\) grid is either filled or empty, and has up to eight adjacent neighboring squares, where neighboring squares share either a side or a corner. The grid is transformed by the following rules:

• Any filled square with two or three filled neighbors remains filled.

• Any empty square with exactly three filled neighbors becomes a filled square.

• All other squares remain empty or become empty.

A sample transformation is shown in the figure below.

[Figure 1](figures/2022_AMC_10B_Q19_question_fig1.svg)

Suppose the \(5 \times 5\) grid has a border of empty squares surrounding a \(3 \times 3\) subgrid. How many initial configurations will lead to a transformed grid consisting of a single filled square in the center after a single transformation? (Rotations and reflections of the same configuration are considered different.)

[Figure 2](figures/2022_AMC_10B_Q19_question_fig2.svg)

solutions.explanation:
The center neighbors every other square of the inner \(3\times3\) subgrid. If it starts empty, it needs exactly three filled neighbors. If it starts filled, it needs two or three filled neighbors. Thus there must initially be either three filled squares, or four filled squares including the center. All neighbor counts refer to the initial grid.

First rule out four filled squares. Besides the center, there would be three filled squares around it. If any two of those three are neighbors, each has at least two and at most three filled neighbors, including the center, so an unwanted square survives. Therefore those three squares must be pairwise nonneighboring.

If all three are corners, two occupy the ends of one side of the subgrid. If one is a side midpoint, its only nonneighbors around the center are the three squares on the opposite side; the only nonneighboring pair among those is the two corners. In either situation, two filled corners lie on the same side, and the midpoint between them is empty. That midpoint neighbors those two corners and the center, but not the third outer filled square. It therefore becomes filled. So four filled squares cannot work.

Now suppose exactly three squares start filled. A square is filled after the transformation exactly when the square together with its neighbors contains all three initial filled squares: an initially empty square then has three filled neighbors, while an initially filled square has two.

Consequently, the three chosen squares must reach both the top and bottom rows, and both the left and right columns, of the inner subgrid. These conditions are sufficient because a neighborhood containing squares in both extreme rows must be centered in the middle row; the same argument forces its column to be the middle column. They are also necessary. For example, if the top row contains no filled square, the neighborhood of the square immediately below the center also contains all three initial filled squares, producing an extra filled square. The other missing sides work similarly. This argument also checks the surrounding border.

Count triples satisfying these four conditions.

If a triple contains two diagonally opposite corners, choose that corner pair in \(2\) ways and the third square in \(7\) ways. A triple cannot contain both opposite-corner pairs, so this gives \(2\cdot7=14\) configurations.

Suppose there is no opposite-corner pair. There must be at least one corner, because without corners, reaching all four sides would require all four side midpoints. There cannot be three corners, because any three corners contain an opposite pair.

With exactly two corners, they must be the endpoints of one side. The third square must reach the opposite side, and either corner there would create an opposite-corner pair. Thus it must be that side's midpoint. There are \(4\) choices for the side containing the two corners.

With exactly one corner, the other two squares must be the midpoints of the two sides opposite that corner. For example, the upper-left corner requires the bottom and right midpoints. There are \(4\) choices for the corner.

These cases are exhaustive and disjoint, and the choices count different orientations separately. The total is
\[
14+4+4=\boxed{22},
\]
which is choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
solutions.title: Count triples that reach all four sides
